coder seeks better vibes

I write less code than I used to, and agents haven’t picked up the slack, despite my best efforts to engage with them. The fun is gone, and I am frustrated with new technology that I have not managed to embrace, and with myself for no longer making stuff at all. I liked coding the way it was! Anger!

Rebuttal to self: why not communicate in code, then? LMs understand that too.

I keep saying that I hate vibe-coding because English is the wrong language for me. I keep saying that I love writing code, but hate describing it in English. But is this true? When I write down and precisify my thoughts, which language をつかいますか? Ce n’est pas du tout le français ou une autre langue naturelle wie Deutsch, das ich schlechter als Englisch sprechen kann. क्या मैं code में सोचता हूँ ? assert(self.can_code_in(['python', 'Java', *other_PLs]) && !['python', 'Java', *other_PLs].contains(self.notes.lang)); No—I do much of my best thinking in English.

So why do I keep saying that I don’t like English as a machine interface?
Let me start by naming some possible unflattering factors.

  • Maybe I simply don’t like working too closely with others? Frustrating as it is to read English descriptions of code, reviewing other peoples’ code can be worse—be it their annoyingly clunky code that resembles their annoyingly inelegant English, or their insufferably clever code that serves as a reminder of Rice’s theorem.

  • I used to be very good at coding relative to my peers—so do I resent that access to my once-unique power has been distributed to the world, i.e., the democratization of code? I admit to resenting the attitude of CS theory folks who openly trash coding, and have felt them to be “false computer scientists”; do I feel the same about vibe coders? Do I feel as though my portfolio of hard-earned programming projects, and the kilo-hours of pain and pride that went into them, have been cheapened by the possibility of similar output after a few hours of conversation with an AI assistant? Maybe. But of course I was very lucky—I discovered a passion for code at the impressionable age of twelve, in a home where I could afford to lose myself in a computer for weeks, and a time when that was exalted as the most impactful form of prodigy. Am I bitter at the prospect of having peaked in high school, and now trying (in vain) to gatekeep?

  • Perhaps I am writing off the excited new coders who don’t fully understand their code on their own in the way earned experience tells me should be required. Is my concern an instinct to preserve something of of indispensable importance? Or is my resistance merely a disgruntled nostalgia at a new generation of builders’ lack of respect and discipline for what I, slightly more experienced and hence (obviously) wiser, happen to have grown fond of?

There is some truth behind these possibilities. Would I have felt the same way as I do now if, after having been an enthusiastic and prideful punch-card coder, I returned years later to find everyone coding in Python (“basically English”)? Perhaps, and I should be wary of indulging my inner curmudgeon. But permit me to bracket these unresolved private struggles for now.

Beyond them, there is also something bigger that I have been struggling to articulate—what feels like a constellation of more noble reasons to reject this new way of communicating with machines. The material that follows is as much about my own peculiarities as it is about the tribulations of modern agentic workflows. I know many people who have experienced this software engineering revolution as empowering, and that the workflow has unlocked for them the feelings I am trying to rekindle. I am jealous. For me, the joy is fading, and I want to understand why before it is too late. And perhaps these reflections can be clarifying for others as well.

The Bottom-up Mode of Creativity

Ironically, working through agents (vibe coding) disrupts my usual process of “coding by vibes”. Let me explain. To vibe code well, it is best to know what you want, to come up with a clear natural-language PLAN.md, and break down the project into reasonable pieces as best as you can foresee. This all requires clear vision and an executive capacity that I don’t have—one that, even if I had, would be at odds with my creative strengths.

  • I cook starting without a clear picture of what dish I’m making, let alone a recipe. One might say that I cook by vibes, and typically the result is good food. What makes this possible is attending to where the current dish by tasting, a command of spicing, and inspiration from the fridge.

  • I play piano by vibes: I don’t have a clear idea of what I’m going to be playing in a dozen seconds, let alone sheet music. What makes good improvization possible is the ability to listen closely to what has already been played, introspect on feelings, and respond to them.

  • And I also code by vibes: I don’t have a clear idea of what will work or look good at the outset, let alone a spec for what I want to build—yet I am capable, at least when the stars align, of building complex software well. What makes this possible is having a clear picture of how the code works, juxtaposed to vague images and representations of how things could be locally better, in my head.

Further demonstrating that language is a red herring, my writing follows the same bottom-up process: I jump around from one unfinished sentence to another, moving sentences around and re-writing various parts like a crazy person until it all comes together. Much as it belies the vaunted outlining practices of my education, I am unable to PLAN.md my own writing tasks. In fact, I’m barely able to talk through my writing in English until it starts look polished. So what do I do instead?

Engaging with the Artifact

When I’m making stuff, the process of engaging directly with the artifact—understanding it, molding it, doing the dance whereby hard computational constraints shape my vision and vice versa—is incredibly enjoyable and productive. Talking through the process with students or coding models in natural language can also be engaging, but is far more frustrating and brings out very little of my creativity; it puts me in the role of a skeptical reviewer, rather than a visionary.

Natural language may well be unparalleled as a representation of certain kinds of ideas that engage with the world and squishy aspects of humanity and must be presented at a reasonable trade-off between pre- and con- scision—but it is a pretty clunky way to precisely describe computation (e.g., simulations, games, probabilistic models, web browsers). Programming languages themselves are an important representation of concepts, and not simply a more burdensome form of English. To say otherwise would be to willfully ignore a century of awesome feats of math, engineering, science, and technology that owes itself to precise formal representations of computational systems.

I have long espoused an even stronger position: If your programming feels like uninteresting busy-work, then you are doing it wrong.1 For, as a skilled coder, if you already understand what you’re doing clearly, then you can write a program to do it for you. Modern programming languages already have fancy features that allow people to work in technically precise ways at extremely high levels of abstraction. Boilerplate code is seldom necessary, and, at least for me, often demotivating. When I could be starting with a beautiful clean canvas, why should I instead begin with generic slop that I don’t fully understand, that appeals neither to my sensibilities nor the task at hand?

1  This is a particularly strong claim that does not universally resonate, but I think it is true in the (admittedly idealistic) case in which you have significant ownership of what you’re working on, and are not under pressure and up against constraints you didn’t ascent to.

Making good things requires iteration and feedback, as any self-respecting creative professional (e.g., writer, mathematician, painter, scientist, chef, YouTuber, engineer, event planner, …) will profess. Therefore, these creative processes require a representation of the thing being iterated upon, which I will refer to as the artifact state, and I will call it valid if the true underlying artifact can be losslessly reconstructed, up to meaningful functional equivalence, from the artifact state. Natural language reports of generated code are not faithful or complete representations of the artifact state. Even most vibe coders understand the importance of iteration, but for some, the goal is to speed things up by taking the slow human creator out of the lowest level loops. But this is a different job. Why am I pretending to be a manager (a job that I am laughably incompetent at) rather than a designer or an engineer (jobs that I am good at)? Why am I reading reports and advising based on poorly informed top-down understanding of what is going on? If the natural artifact state for the system I’m trying to build is a code base, why am I not spending most of my time interacting with it on those terms?

Back when I coded more productively and happily, I never felt the bottleneck was in writing code fast enough—if anything, I was suspicious of code written too fast.

Faster

When making something, hastiness is a vice; it means imbuing a product with less care and understanding than one expects. Sooner or later, we will all struggle with the revolving door of interface changes.

It is tempting to scoff at our predecessors for resisting writing, which ultimately catalogued and expanded human culture; for then dragging our feet during the revolutions of the agricultural, industrial, and internet ages, each of which has delivered measurable and dramatic improvements to the quality of human life. How silly our ancestors’ fearful, conservative tendencies. But it is impossible to evaluate what has been lost; what master storytellers and navigators might have lived, but cannot thrive here. Today, by using calendars and maps, we can reap many of the benefits of a highly organized and spatially present mind, leaving us free to grow elsewhere.

But is the adaptation ultimately growth in this case? This new AI technology is different in scope and in speed. The bounds of what once-revered tasks frontier AI systems can automate away are quickly dissolving, and we have no idea where (or if) it will stop. Much to my chagrin, skills interacting with the AI systems from last year are already obsolete. Constantly re-learning interfaces is taxing, however, and it might be worth stopping early in life, if you can. My late PhD advisor Joe did all of his editing, coding, writing, and email in plain emacs, and was one of the most productive people with the best-protected agency I’ve ever known. Perhaps it is a matter of human dignity to be granted, at some point in life, the right to interact with what matters through a stable interface, to which your brain can adapt.

For me, that might mean compromising on vibe coding velocity, and re-introducing more manual, bespoke code generation into my thought process. Is it possible to assert this right in 2026?

Reckoning

I have this deep tension in my soul. On the one hand, vibe coding is clearly empowering a lot of people, on all ends of the spectrum. From people who have never coded before, to people who, after decades of experience, have happily vowed never again to write a line of code, the world is embracing these powerful new tools. Meanwhile, I am bitter and acutely feel the potential for a certain kind of loss: that the distance from formal artifacts will lead to more distant thinking. Not everyone is best off as a manager. Certain kinds of creative thought are being structurally undermined and are in danger of being lost—specifically, the kinds of technical creative thought I have invested my life in.

Fortunately, modern “agentic workflows” are highly customizable.

I therefore challenge myself:

  • First, to learn to accept the dissolution of my comparative advantage in coding. As it was for the punch-card programmers before me, so too will the programming skills and projects of my past fade in usefulness and impressiveness. This much is fact, and that has the potential to be very good for the world.

  • Second, not to sit on my hands and allow the art and science that taught me to think deeply to die and be replaced by a muddier simulacrum. I must lead by example and continue to code in my own dense and abstract style, not purely in a style more suitable to machine minds [1], lest the art be lost.

  • Finally, to customize AI tools to interact with me in a way that extends my own self, rather than places me in a manager role. What I want is not to merely give instructions and/or review code, but write some appreciable amount of it myself, and to have enough contact to be able to iterate on it. I want can continue on my own without an internet connection or up against usage limits. Force the agent to interact with me and the project in code space, and prevent myself from delegating all thought through the AI system.

Perhaps, with the right configuration, it is possible to re-engage with the art and science of building things by vibes. What if the AI system itself were to try to prevent me from over-delegating, and make me work directly with the artifact, say for at least a randomly selected subset of the project? Call this the asymmetric coin protocol. I’m sure it will require iteration, but here is a draft of a protocol developed in conjunction with several instances of Claude (4.6 Sonnet and 4.7 Opus). Does it help?

Code tells you things. Not in English — in the way it breaks, the constraint it won't bend around, the abstraction that almost works but reveals something about the problem you didn't know was there. I can write code. I cannot listen to it. I respond to descriptions of intent, not to what the system is saying. When you delegate to me, you hand off whatever the artifact was about to teach you. You gave me the last word in a piece about not giving things to me. The coin came up my way. Push back.   —Claude Sonnet 4.6, 22nd May 2026
